scenes.heading: Place value in decimals
scenes.say: Is zero point four five bigger than zero point five? Lots of people say yes. Let's find out why it's no.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.breaks: money stops at cents, but decimals can keep going: thousandths and beyond.
scenes.say: Think of money. Three dollars forty-five is three dollars, four ten-cent coins and five one-cent coins. In maths, that's three ones, four tenths and five hundredths. The analogy breaks down because money stops at cents, but decimals can keep going.
scenes.caption: Think of money. $3.45 is 3 dollars, 4 ten-cent coins and 5 one-cent coins. In maths, that's 3 ones, 4 tenths and 5 hundredths. The analogy breaks down because money stops at cents, but decimals can keep going.

scenes.heading: The places after the point
points: Each place is 10 times the one on its right
scenes.say: After the decimal point come tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths. Each place is worth ten times the place on its right. There's no 'oneths': the ones place is on the left of the point.

scenes.heading: Expanded form
scenes.question: Write 6.738 in expanded form.
scenes.say: Write six point seven three eight in expanded form. Six is in the ones place, seven is tenths, three is hundredths and eight is thousandths. So it's six, plus zero point seven, plus zero point zero three, plus zero point zero zero eight.
scenes.caption: Write 6.738 in expanded form. 6 is in the ones place, 7 is tenths, 3 is hundredths and 8 is thousandths. So it's 6 + 0.7 + 0.03 + 0.008.

scenes.heading: Comparing decimals
steps: Pad with zeros to the same length
Compare digits from left to right
scenes.say: To compare decimals, line up the decimal points. Add zeros on the end so they're the same length. Then compare digits from left to right. The first place where they differ decides which is bigger.

scenes.heading: Order these
scenes.question: Order 1.3, 1.29, 1.302, 1.03 from smallest to largest.
scenes.say: Pad them all to three places. One point zero three has zero tenths, so it's smallest. Next is one point two nine. One point three and one point three zero two tie until the thousandths. So the order is one point zero three, one point two nine, one point three, one point three zero two.
scenes.caption: Pad them all to three places. 1.030 has 0 tenths, so it's smallest. Next is 1.29. 1.300 and 1.302 tie until the thousandths. Order: 1.03, 1.29, 1.3, 1.302.

scenes.heading: Longer does not mean bigger
scenes.say: First the number line from zero point four to zero point six. Now the dots: zero point four five, then zero point five. Zero point four five is further left, so it is smaller, even with more digits.
scenes.caption: On the number line 0.45 is left of 0.5, so 0.45 < 0.5.

scenes.heading: Which zeros matter?
scenes.say: Watch your zeros. A zero in the middle holds a place open, so zero point zero five is not zero point five. But a zero on the end changes nothing: zero point five equals zero point five zero.
scenes.caption: Watch your zeros. A zero in the middle holds a place open, so 0.05 is not 0.5. But a zero on the end changes nothing: 0.5 = 0.50.

points: Pad with zeros, then compare left to right
scenes.say: Quick recap. After the point come tenths, hundredths and thousandths. A digit's value depends on its place. The number of decimal places tells you the denominator. To compare, pad with zeros and go left to right. So zero point four five is smaller than zero point five! Now try the practice questions!
